sections.title: Seismic Deformation Analysis
sections.summary: Alternatively, a Newmark-type analysis finds the yield acceleration ky (FS = 1.0) for surfaces behind the anchors and estimates permanent displacement from ky/PGA (Figure 58, Hynes and Franklin 1984) or a formal Newmark analysis, using the free field PGA.
sections.body: As an alternative to pseudo-static design, external stability may be assessed by a Newmark-type seismic deformation analysis: a pseudo-static analysis gives the yield acceleration ky for surfaces behind the anchors, the smallest horizontal seismic coefficient reducing the factor of safety to 1.0. The ratio of ky to PGA gives the permanent displacement from design charts (Figure 58, p. 119, after Hynes and Franklin, 1984; upper bound, mean and mean plus one standard deviation) or a formal Newmark analysis (FHWA-SA-97-076, 1997). Use the free field PGA, which includes local site effects and better represents average acceleration over the excavation height than the amplified top-of-wall PGA. The heading is printed "5.10.3.2Seismic Deformation Analysis". (pp. 118 to 119)

sections.title: Wall and Ground Movements
sections.summary: In sands and stiff clays lateral wall movement averages about 0.2 percent H (maximum 0.5 percent H) and settlement behind the wall about 0.15 percent H (maximum 0.5 percent H); Figure 59 gives settlement profiles, Curves I and II for permanent walls. Flat anchors and adequate axial capacity limit settlement.
sections.body: Movement control needs vary: permanent walls in granular soils with no nearby structures pose little concern, but movement may be the main issue for urban temporary excavation support. Estimates come from semi-empirical performance data. In sands and stiff clays maximum lateral wall movement averages about 0.2%H with a maximum of about 0.5%H (H wall height), and maximum settlement behind the wall averages about 0.15%H with a maximum of about 0.5%H. Figure 59 (p. 120) gives settlement profiles behind braced and anchored walls (settlement/depth of excavation against distance/depth of excavation): Curve I sands, Curve II stiff to very hard clays, Curve III soft to medium clays; Curves I and II are commonly used for permanent anchored walls; settlements increase rapidly in soft to medium clays with marginal basal stability. Movements (p. 120): (1) cantilever movement before the first anchor, (2) wall settlement mobilizing end bearing, (3) elastic tendon elongation with load increase, (4) anchor yielding or load redistribution in the bond zone, (5) mass movement behind the anchors; the last three translate the wall and are small in competent soils. Excessive vertical settlement may cause significant lateral movement and high wall/anchor interface stresses; minimize it with flat anchors and an embedded portion designed for the axial loads. (pp. 119 to 120)

sections.title: Drainage Systems for Anchored Walls and Slopes
sections.summary: Subsurface water is collected by prefabricated drainage elements between lagging and CIP facing (or gravel behind precast facing), led to collector pipes or weepholes; horizontal drains have limits; surface water is diverted by grading, ditches, dikes or extended wall elements.
sections.body: With cast-in-place (CIP) facing, subsurface flow is usually collected by prefabricated drainage elements between wall and lagging, full length elements attached to the lagging at final grade or single strips at designed spacings. With shotcrete instead of timber lagging, prefabricated vertical drains are spiked against the soil in segments, spliced by shingling with an overlap of one strip width. With precast facing the space between temporary face and facing may be gravel-filled as the drainage element. Water flows down to collector pipes or out through the facing in longitudinal/outlet pipes or weepholes. Where flows are large, horizontal drains, small diameter perforated pipes in nearly horizontal holes (p. 121), may relieve trapped water (e.g., a wall at the base of a steep slope), extending beyond the critical surface; but (1) install them only at final grade unless a perched water table exists, (2) control alignment to avoid the anchors, no splaying from one entry point, (3) they usually cannot lower water to finished grade, as equipment height sets the lowest elevation and drains slope upward, (4) effluent collection needs special design for aesthetics. Surface water is directed away by grading, ditches or pipes; dikes near the top or wall elements extended above grade keep it out of the excavation. (pp. 120 to 121)

sections.title: Wall System Appurtenances
sections.summary: Identify utilities, drainage, traffic barriers, parapets and noise walls early; nearby utilities may be damaged by wall deformation and affect anchor inclination and spacing; barrier loads (AASHTO 1996) and noise wall foundations must be designed.
sections.body: Existing and proposed appurtenances can significantly affect design, construction and cost and should be identified early: (1) underground utilities and drainage, (2) traffic barriers and parapet walls, (3) noise walls. The site investigation should locate all facilities; nearby telephone cables and gas and water lines may be overstressed by abrupt vertical and horizontal wall deformation, requiring relocation or protection that adds time and cost, and their location influences anchor inclination, spacing and construction sequence. Earth pressures from barrier and parapet dead weight and impact loads must be included (AASHTO, 1996) (p. 122). Noise wall foundations resist wind loads; noise walls may be cast integrally with or founded independently of the anchored wall. (pp. 121 to 122)

sections.title: Resisting the Upper Anchor Test Load
sections.summary: Always check passive capacity at the uppermost anchor: Fp = 1.125 Kp gamma h1^2 s (Eq. 48, FHWA-RD-97-103), developed over 1.5 times the anchor depth; the allowable value, Fp/1.5, must exceed the upper anchor test load.
sections.body: Where the ground behind the upper wall is disturbed or the anchor load is high, the soldier beam may deflect excessively while the upper anchor is tested; the ground behind the beam must develop enough passive resistance, and for all designs the passive capacity at the uppermost anchor must be checked. The required passive capacity of the beam may be calculated by Eq. 48 (FHWA-RD-97-103, 1998), assuming passive resistance Fp develops over 1.5 times the depth to the upper anchor; Kp from Figure 16 or 17, h1 the depth to the upper anchor, s the horizontal spacing. A factor of safety of 1.5 on the maximum capacity gives the allowable resistance, which should exceed the upper anchor test load. (p. 122)
key_points: Check passive capacity at the uppermost anchor for all walls (p. 122).
Fp = 1.125 Kp gamma h1^2 s (Eq. 48) over 1.5 h1 (p. 122).
Allowable = Fp/1.5, greater than the upper anchor test load (p. 122).

sections.title: Anchored Walls for Fill Applications
sections.summary: Bottom-up fill anchored walls apply only to rehabilitation: backfill and stress anchors in stages, restressing to lock-off; design for actual (theoretical) earth pressures; use select backfill and light compaction. Where standard testing is impossible, test preproduction anchors to 200 percent.
sections.body: Highway anchored walls are usually built top-down; bottom-up construction in fill applies only to rehabilitating existing walls (FHWA-DP-90-068-003, 1990), new fill walls usually being mechanically stabilized earth. Sequence for two levels: install soldier beams (or confirm the existing wall can take the anchor loads); backfill and lag to about midheight between the anchor levels; install the bottom anchors; stress them without significant inward wall movement, possibly below lock-off (p. 123); backfill to at least 1 m above the top anchors; restress the bottom anchors to lock-off; install and temporarily stress the top anchors; backfill to finished grade; restress the top anchors to lock-off. Use select backfill compacted at low energy with small equipment to protect tendons; poor backfill settlement bends anchors at the connection, which they are not designed for. Design loads are earth pressures with the wall fully backfilled and surcharged; early anchors may not be testable to 133 percent, so they are stressed to a small nominal load and locked off, and restressed as backfill rises; after finished grade they may be tested to 133 percent if passive resistance and the face allow. Anchors carry actual earth pressure loads rather than apparent envelopes, wall movement following theoretical envelopes. Where standard testing is impossible, install preproduction anchors in similar ground, performance test them and load to 200 percent of production design load; passing implies production anchors would pass at 133 percent. (pp. 122 to 123)
